title: For five years, nobody wanted it. Silver promoted the adhesive inside 3M as a solution without a
description:
3M scientist. He tried to make a super strong adhesive and made a weak, reusable one instead.

Silver promoted the adhesive inside 3M as a solution without a problem and found no supporters. It had been aimed at the aerospace industry.

Heard Silver's seminar, then used the adhesive to hold a bookmark in his hymn book.

In 1977 3M test marketed it as "Press 'n Peel" in four cities, and the results were disappointing. In 1978 free samples went to offices in Boise, Idaho, and over 90 per cent of recipients said they would buy it.

The yellow was chance. It matched the scrap paper in the next lab.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-it_Note (read in full): established that Spencer Silver made a low tack reusable adhesive at 3M in 1968 while trying to make a strong one, that he promoted it internally for five years as a solution without a problem, that Art Fry used it for hymn book bookmarks in 1974 under 3M's permitted bootlegging policy, that the 1977 test market as "Press 'n Peel" was disappointing, that a 1978 free sample campaign in Boise, Idaho, led to over 90 per cent saying they would buy it, that the national launch was in 1980, and that the canary yellow came from scrap paper in the next lab.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Fry (read): independently established that Fry attended Silver's seminar and thought of using the adhesive to anchor a bookmark in his hymn book, that 3M's policy lets employees spend some work time on projects of their choosing, and that Post-it Notes were released to the national market in 1980.
